note: Every high-severity finding the public corpus produced on 2026-09-13, read
against the cited source and given one of three verdicts.
true-positive  - a real defect, or a warning a reviewer would defend.
false-positive - the code is correct (or the severity is not defensible);
`guard` names the documented guard that should have
caught it, so the fix has an address.
unsure         - the reviewer could not settle it from the source alone.
`state` exists so the file is a ratchet rather than a permanent red light:
open  - the analyzer still produces this false positive. `check` lists it
and does not fail on it (pass --strict to make it fail).
fixed - the analyzer no longer produces it. If it ever comes back,
`check` fails: that is the regression half of the ratchet.
A high finding whose key is absent from this file always fails `check` -
nobody has read it yet, and an unread high finding is the one thing this
corpus exists to stop.
Keys are `repo|CODE|repo-relative file|symbol`, so they survive an edit
above the finding and do not depend on which target happened to find it.
A path under `.mlview/notebooks/` is the module MLView generates from a
notebook under --include-notebooks (CONTRACTS 11.29); it is the same defect
as its .py twin where the repo ships both.

scikit-learn|MLV101|examples/release_hig.why: `sfs.fit(X, y)` at line 153 fits a SequentialFeatureSelector on iris, bound by `X, y = load_iris(...)` at line 149. The `train_test_split(X, y, ...)` MLView cited is at line 180, twenty-seven lines and one `X, y = fetch_covtype(...)` later: a different dataset in a different section of the same sphinx-gallery script. There is no split of the iris data anywhere in the file, so there is nothing to leak into.
scikit-learn|MLV101|examples/release_hig.guard: PUB-03's `_rebound_between` is the guard, and it read `AssignRecord.targets` through `dotted_text`, which is empty for an `ast.Tuple`. `X, y = load_iris(...)` is therefore invisible to it, and tuple unpacking is how every scikit-learn example binds its data.
scikit-learn|MLV101|examples/release_hig.repro: mlview analyze <scratch>/repro/sfs (19 lines: load_iris into sfs.fit, then fetch_covtype into train_test_split)
scikit-learn|MLV101|examples/release_hig.fixedWhy: PUB-15, fixed in hardening round 1: `_target_names` flattens tuple, list and starred assignment targets, so the guard PUB-03 added for `X = ...` now also sees `X, y = ...`. The finding is gone in both modes and an `untagged_dataflow` coverage note names the rebinding line, so the silence is declared rather than quiet.

PythonDataScienceHandbook|MLV102|noteboo.why: Cell 16 is hand-rolled two-fold cross-validation: `y2_model = model.fit(X1, y1).predict(X2)` then `y1_model = model.fit(X2, y2).predict(X1)`. MLView reported the second line at high / certain 0.97, called a KNeighborsClassifier "the transformer", and said the held-out score is not an estimate of unseen-data performance - about a model whose only score is computed on the half it was never fitted on. Both statements are false, on one of the most-read notebooks in the corpus.
PythonDataScienceHandbook|MLV102|noteboo.guard: ROB-10 / PUB-02 established `_is_transformer_fit` because `sklearn.base.BaseEstimator.fit` carries the role FIT, so every estimator fit is a candidate. MLV101 calls it; MLV102 did not, although its title, `why` and `fix_hint` are all about a transformer and every `expected` MLV102 label in the labelled corpus is a `fit_transform` on one.
PythonDataScienceHandbook|MLV102|noteboo.repro: mlview analyze <scratch>/repro/kfold (16 lines: the two swapped fit/predict statements)
PythonDataScienceHandbook|MLV102|noteboo.fixedWhy: PUB-14, fixed in hardening round 1: MLV102 now asks `_is_transformer_fit` the same question MLV101 has asked since ROB-10, one mechanism rather than two. Every labelled MLV102 number is unchanged to four decimal places in both dataflow modes (recall 0.8000), and the public corpus drops from 37 high findings to 34.

yolov5|MLV402|utils/loss.py|self.loss_fc.why: The code is correct. `self.loss_fcn` is nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss and it is fed the raw logits `pred` at line 26; the `pred = torch.sigmoid(pred)` on line 27 rebinds the local AFTER the loss has been computed and is only used to build the blur factor. MLView's own message gives the bug away: it cites a producer at line 27 for a use at line 26.
yolov5|MLV402|utils/loss.py|self.loss_fc.guard: MLV402 `_final_producer` (analyzer/src/mlview/rules/r_loss.py) takes the scope's last binding for the argument name instead of the binding that reaches the call site; a producer whose loc is strictly after the use, with no loop enclosing both, cannot have produced that value.
yolov5|MLV402|utils/loss.py|self.loss_fc.repro: mlview issues <scratch>/repro/bce  (12-line file, see the report)
yolov5|MLV402|utils/loss.py|self.loss_fc.fixedWhy: PUB-01, fixed in hardening round 1: `arg_ref` now resolves an argument against the store in effect at the call's own line (`binding_of(..., at=)`, REV-01's ordered lookup), so the `pred = torch.sigmoid(pred)` written one line BELOW the loss no longer reads as its producer.

keras-io|MLV121|examples/vision/pointnet.why: `dataset.shuffle(len(train_points))` at 153, then `dataset.take(n)` -> train and `dataset.skip(n)` -> validation at 156-157. tf.data reshuffles every epoch by default, so the train/validation partition changes on every pass and validation rows are trained on. A real defect in a published Keras example.

mlflow|MLV401|examples/pytorch/CaptumExa.why: TitanicSimpleNNModel.forward returns `self.softmax(self.linear3(...))` (nn.Softmax at line 80) and the loss at 165 is nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which log-softmaxes again. The classic double-softmax defect, correctly traced across the class boundary.

pytorch_geometric|MLV301|examples/lcm_ag.why: `test(loader)` is decorated @torch.no_grad() but never calls model.eval(), and `train()` never calls model.train() either, so the LCM model - which holds torch.nn.Dropout in both its encoder (line 97) and its decoder (line 105) - is evaluated with dropout active. The printed Val Acc is noise-inflated.

scikit-learn|MLV101|examples/application.why: A defensible warning rather than a bug: `X = MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(X)` at 41 is value-identical to the `X` that `train_test_split` consumes at 56, so the scaler's min and max do see the held-out rows. Harmless on USPS pixels, and the rule is right about the shape.

wandb-examples|MLV301|examples/pytorch/p.why: The accuracy loop over test_loader runs inside the training loop with neither model.eval() nor torch.no_grad(), and CNNModel holds nn.Dropout(p=config.dropout) (line 49). The accuracy that is logged to W&B is measured with dropout on.

note: A sample of medium findings, read the same way. `check` does not gate on
these - medium is allowed to be wrong sometimes by design - but a medium
false positive that asserts a falsehood about the code is still a bug, and
three of these do.

rows.why: `ts_cv` is a TimeSeriesSplit. MLView says it 'shuffles rows that look like a time series' and offers the fix 'Use TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=...)' - it is telling the user to do what the code already does, and the claim that TimeSeriesSplit shuffles is false.
rows.guard: MLV106 must exclude SPLIT-role calls whose receiver resolves to an order-preserving splitter (TimeSeriesSplit, and by the same argument GroupKFold / LeaveOneGroupOut). The `shuffle=False` guard on train_test_split works - line 124 of the same file fires correctly and line 133 does not.

rows.why: PPOLightning sets `self.automatic_optimization = False` at line 196 and its training_step calls self.manual_backward and steps both optimizers itself. Returning nothing is correct under manual optimization. MLView says 'Lightning has nothing to back-propagate and the batch is skipped' at medium / 0.90, above the Problems-panel floor. MLV706 already knows about manual optimization and stayed silent, so the gate exists and MLV707 does not use it.
rows.guard: MLV707 must skip a LightningModule whose __init__ assigns `self.automatic_optimization = False`, or whose training_step calls self.manual_backward.

rows.why: `psnr = 10 * log10(1 / mse.item())` is a Python float - `.item()` is already applied and math.log10 cannot return a tensor. MLView says 'avg_psnr accumulates the tensor psnr ... keeps its autograd graph alive', which is false on both counts.
rows.guard: MLV205 should walk the producer chain of the accumulated value and stay silent once it passes through `.item()`, `float()`, or a `math.*` call.

rows.why: Both are Keras programs. MLView tells the user to call `zero_dce_model.eval()` and `test_augmentation.eval()` - methods that do not exist in Keras - and in the second case the 'model' is a keras.Sequential of augmentation layers inside a tf.data map function named test_map_fn. Same name-regex root cause as PUB-05. Confidence lands at 0.20-0.34, below the 0.6 visibility floor, so the Problems panel is spared; the diagram rail is not.
rows.guard: see PUB-05, plus: MLV301 declares frameworks=['torch'] and should not fire where the receiver resolves to a keras object.

rows.why: `DataLoader(dataset1, **train_kwargs)` where shuffle=True is merged in at line 113 only when `use_accel` is true. On CPU the loader really does not shuffle; on an accelerator it does. MLView cannot resolve the **kwargs and says so by landing at confidence 0.59, just under the visibility floor. Defensible either way - recorded here so a later change in either direction is a deliberate one.

Hard-coded `.cuda()` with no availability check. NVIDIA's repository is GPU-only on purpose, so this is advice rather than a defect - which is exactly what medium severity and the rule's portability wording claim.

A random `train_test_split` on a frame whose features are `shift(...)` lags. The example itself goes on to say this is wrong and switches to TimeSeriesSplit; MLView flagged the line the text warns about.
